Offline Blue rectangs are flags. Price makes a bearish decision within the flag. Price exits the flag and another flag is formed. Price exits this flag after a Banned bullish decision is made. Price cps to near the bearish decision and moves south through cp to the bullish decision. There price turns north and takes out the pole of the bearish decision. H[/quote] Posts: 197 Hi Hoto, Thank you received: For me a broken FL is just Broke... If I understand the FTR concept 333 correctly, after price engulfs something important like a FL, it tries to return to origin of the drop/rally and fails. I may not have the best definition of FTR, but for me, if that area that failed does not print a new low/high then it is no FTR and I will steer away from it. Also an FTR can relate to any other important area, be it SR, SD, Swap, another FTR or even a FL. But... IMHO an FTR to a FL has to happen before that FL breaks. FTR should highlight bullish/bearish strength, so it has to happen before the opponent takes control. Now as far as my diagram above is concerned, I was just trying to highlight the relationship of price (after a break of FL) to the limits of that same FL once price retraces back into it in the future. It was just an observation I wanted to share with everyone. It was not meant to confuse anyone... Here is the chart I was tearing apart at the time... Price could break the previous highs, or it may drop to break the lows created by 3. We don't know, we have to wait (on this time frame, anyway). 6. Price returns to the flag, but we don't get a signal to do anything - we trade from the edges of flags/ranges, not the middle. 7. Oh, come on! I'm getting bored, now... Ok, arguably we broke the high at 5, but not the high before that. Was that a fakeout on a lower time frame, into the high before 5? I dunno, but it looks like it might have been. 8. OK, so now we know it was a fakeout, as the IT selling has now engulfed the flag at 3, and is now also the FTB to the flag at 2. Wow. So, we take a long here, targeting the high at 7. 9. The ITs are protecting their position at 7 (where they made the fakeout) and sell right through the flags at 2 and 3, and the low at 8. That's a strong engulf, and now 9 becomes a pretty good FTR. 10. Price flags just under the engulfed area, as it decides what to do next 11. Price breaks down, but does not reach the base of the pole (Aaron ) and so we should look for a short on the FTB to the flag at 10. 12. here's the FTB to that flag. 13. Our target for the short is the low made at 11 14. Errr, it's usually 13 that's missing from airliner rows, etc. Oops. 15. Price has cut right through the supply at 10, and has become demand - we should look to take a long at the top of the zone created by 10. 16. The target for that long is the superb FTR created at 9. We also look to take a short at 16, aiming for the base of the pole. 17. We need to be careful (maybe take some profit) as price returns down to the demand at the 15 flag. In this case it cuts right through. It might even give chance for another short from the underside of the flag 18. The engulf of 2 and 10 by the move to 11 gives us the confidence to aim for 18 as the ultimate target. If I can ever do this (or 50% of it) in reality, I'll be the happiest guy on this site (or any other). This is hopelessly idealised, and I may have some concepts a bit off, so HOME EDUCATION FORUM MORE LOGOUT lend a hand!! Posts: 168 Thank you received: What happens when a FL is engulfed? Engulfed FL is a good sign Price wants to fill the base of the FL pole. This 384 is something I like to use as criteria for an FTR trade setup. Why do some FTB trades at FL's work and others don't? A FLAG should break a key level/area to be considered significant. When a bases pole has momentum coming out of a significant price level, SD Zone, SR Flip, etc, and the FL engulfs a key level/area (SR, SD, FL), this is criteria that is important when considering entering on RT to the FL area. Posts: 941 EDUCATION FORUM MORE LOGOUT after the fact its easier to spot them as you understand, so in real time Thank you reHcOeiMveEd: some are cleaner than others. just work with what you have each time. 2920 ok, for flag limits two things are important. as IF said "they signify the end of the momentum" and also we look for them at previous important areas, like obvious SR for example. why? because after the pole, price tries to get back into the area and fails, making a decision and this is our flag limit. so on first return of the price, since the decision has already been made, we can expect a reaction. also, the flag limit area may hold for more tries than the first visit and is valid till broken (but i dont advise anyone to trade it a 2nd time) after the flag limit is engulfed price is free to travel back to the base of the pole, like in Hotochin's example. Trader Akif, Posts: 84 Thank you received: 44 HOME AtEtaDcUhmCeAnTtsIO: N FORUM MORE LOGOUT THANK YOU QUICK REPLY REPLY QUOTE Flag Limits 29 May 2014 19:47 #584 Kanzler akifusenet, Offline You're asking some very good questions which I was asking myself a month or so ago!! I don't have all the solutions but hopefully what I've Associate Trader learned is of some help. First, about the significance of flag limits...some of them are more "localized" flag limits. For example, FL1 is an engulf of a Posts: 196 local high, while FL2 is more of an engulf of the flag area to the left (where Thank you received: we see price meandering around without any new poles). To me that tells me FL2 is probably the more significant than FL1 since we're engulfing a 350 larger zone. FL3 is another story of price engulfing a smaller flag area, but it did work nicely several times as you see. Now onto the more difficult question which I've been searching for as well...FL2 - was it engulfed or not? I don't think so. First, I'm not entirely sure that FL2 is the actual flag limit or not. On the M1 chart where you can't zoom much farther unless you have a tick chart, it's possible that the actual FL extends closer to the "SR" area. If it doesn't and price did move below it, I still see this as an FTR which would show up on higher time frames as a FL in its own right (they are the same thing). Note how price broke above the S/R, tried to get back in, and then moved above the original breakout high, confirming an FTR. Where would I place the stop? Well, I wouldn't have been completely comfortable with that original FL2 zone for previously mentioned reasons, but if I were, I would have placed it a pip or so below the base of it given this is an M1 chart. If I were stopped out, I would have probably given the FTR a try as well since it's valid too. Others might put it beyond the S/R but that isn't something I care to do. Note how in your bottom center graphic that FL2 may have been exceeded by a pip or so but if you use the FTR area it would have stayed within bounds. Significance of FL/FTR has nothing to do with time but with what kind of flag area was engulfed. Are we looking at a strong engulf of a huge daily flag area or are we looking at price engulfing a local flag on the M1? That's what makes the difference in my experience. Keep in mind this is just my two cents, but I hope it helps. This is an area of interest for me as well. The following user(s) said Thank You: rcmacf, akifusenet Feeling the Bern. Thank you received: EDUCATION FORUM MORE LOGOUT 135 HOME Hi John, this question is bothering many of us, including me. The problem is, we are looking for perfection, for something what works 100% of the time. I think, one is only wasting the time doing it. How many weeks, months, years are we wasting looking for answers in forums with clear rules wich work 100% of the time? This is a process oriented approach and you have some very good rules here which you have to build on. But to do, you have to do your own research. There is no way around it. No short cuts. If you take one rule from marketpedia and and go over charts and use the rule in a consistent manner (you use this rule the same way every time), you will get results in terms of if it works or not, in which circumstances etc. You then come to the conclusion, how to trade it. If it for example doesn't work 80% of the time, that's perfect, because you know that when you do the opposite, it will work What I am trying to say is, stop wasting the time searching for perfection and start working on your own unique style, which will work for you and which you will understand because you have built it from the scratch. The process counts. The other thing which is stopping us from improving is the endless searching for 100% accuracy, when there simply is no need for 100% accuracy. We have to accept that we won't be right every time and that is fine because we can still make money. Take something what you think you understand or what you like and do as detailed research on it as you can, then build on it. The following user(s) said Thank You: cuimingzhao THANK YOU QUICK REPLY REPLY QUOTE HOME EDUCATION FORUM MORE LOGOUT Flag Limits 02 Mar 2015 21:00 #807 smimon Whilst it is true that a FL is formed after the break of any high or low, it does not necessarily make it an important FL. The important ones are the ones that form after the break of important opposing levels. Offline In your chart - what is the significance of the green box? What important opposing level was broken that led to its formation? I see you've drawn on Trader a small box that it broke - presumably off something on M1 - but do you think that the break of a small M1 level is as important as the break of the Posts: 549 highs to the left, at which price spent a long time? Not trying to be Thank you received: patronising, forgive me if it comes off that way, but just trying to get you to think about it. "Look left, and then look left again" is a great IF quote. 1075 Here's the AU move as I see it: Remember, spotting important levels is only half of the battle. Reading the movement of price as well is what gives us the context on which to base decisions. Just a zone by itself is only half of the equation. Try not to get too hung up on "needing" to always find exact single tiny FLs on M1. You will drive yourself mad. Instead, find the big obvious ones on higher timeframes, draw a box around the whole FL, and try to focus on just reading the movement of price as it approaches, and look for any surges that give us a clue to when the big boys have entered the market. How did it approach the zone? Did it surge into it? Did it CP? What was the direction of the last large surge in price, bullish or bearish? Have we reached the best level to turn price from, and therefore can we expect a FO? Have we reached the base of the move yet? Is the FL we are looking HOME EDUCATION FORUM MORE LOGOUT at inside daily supply/demand? H4? Weekly? Remember the RTM method is pieces of a jigsaw which all must be pieced together to make full sense of price movement. Focusing exclusively on just one part will cause you to miss the bigger picture. Quite often if we are patient, price will tell us what it wants to do, and we can just get along for the ride. Posts: 106 It can be confusing at first, hopefully this will clear it up for you. Plus it won't Thank you received: hurt to re-read the FTR article 171 FLs are not exactly FTRs. FL's contain FTRs. FL's ecompass the whole HOME EDUCATION FORUM MORE LOGOUT range of hesitation after engulf. FTR's are decision points within FL to continue. FTR's are decision points that happen either before or after engulf. So, for FLs we are interested in DP to continue after engulf. Naturally, when there is an engulf, we can find an FTR (a DP to engulf), and then we can find a FL, that contains a DP to continue (which is also an FTR, but we say it's an FL to point out the difference). Sometimes we can't find an FL, because we have a fakeout and price reverses. HOME EDUCATION FORUM MORE LOGOUT Yes so price retested that CP because the break of a CP makes also an FTR, and price bounced from there down. To trade a FL you have to do what the price reading article says, you have to dissect the level in LTF to make sure there are still some orders left there and also the HTF picture. Then of course watch the approach to the level in LTF for clues like compression, engulfs etc... As you see to do this, you need all the other pieces of this puzzle (CP, engulf, QM,...). Just focus on each one until you can identify them without troubles and then once you know your tools you can study how they interact with each other. Brox wrote: Jurij, you have marked a blue rectangle. But isn't it a FTR? And red line on the second screenshort. Price breaks it and Fails to Return. I am marking only FLs Yes sure it is also an FTR. Every FL is also an FTR, but not every FTR is a FL, this is what has been said many times around in the forums here. FTR means only that price broke some kind of barrier (SR, FL, just a high/low, supply/demand, swap zone) and failed to return (meaning, failed to return back inside that broken zone). My thoughts coincide with 2) - "we don't actually know which set of orders in the flag limit may turn price. It could either be the mouth, body or MPL". Of course as is mentioned the MPL is absolutely the best trade, and I mostly prefer to wait for these orders as well, but we have no guarantees that price will reach the last remaining orders there. If I am to take a trade at the mouth of a FL, it will depend on the size of the FL; with good space provided by PA to allow a trade down to a first target, and a tight FL, we have the luxury of a smaller stop loss, - since whatever the scenario, one thing is certain, my stop must go above the FL we're reacting to. For larger FLs, I'd much rather wait for the MPL of the FL. This is mainly for trade management, and keeping my stops tighter. With nothing to the left, I don't yet see a reason why we can assume that price will necessarily want the MPL, when the ITs may well have all their orders filled by the time price hits the kink to the mouth of the FL, or any possible free pockets of liquidity in the body on the way to the MPL.. This is where I am at with my thinking on this, and of course welcome more thoughts and opinions to build a solid framework for all of this! How do I reslove this? 1373 Hi mate, its best to discuss these issues here which go to the core of the methodology as opposed to the other place. The terms kink/ftr/fl get used a lot. I simplify it by looking at it like this (we all need to take the teachings and use them how we see it). Harry recently HOME EDUCATION FORUM MORE LOGOUT said the articles were written so you can train your eyes (or similar) as opposed to a play by play, which we dont want anyway. I hope this helps. I would ask any other member to also share their view. But after hundreds of hours looking at kinks/FTRs/Kinks in the charts this is what I believe to be true 1. the kink is the actual bump or hiccup itself. (at the very pip or tick price crosses a barrier) -Once I sense there could be a kink. I go looking for it. Sometimes its on that same TF other times it will be on the 1 min or ticks. 2.the kink retraces fails to return and passes the mouth in the direction it was heading after the break. Ergo,. The FTR is formed; 3. Once the above conditions are met the FL is only confirmed once the opposing TG is hit. If any of what I said gels or makes sense, draw up some charts and post here so we can all discuss. Remember there will be times where you will NOT be able to find the above FTR/FL. Its been said before, if we are not there watching price as it breaks the decision could be anyhwere in the entire candle that breaks the area. This is something THAT is so important, because thats how the IT's hide their foot prints and a new high or low forms. I have seen many students draw this hook as the FTR when in fact its the FTB to the FTR/FL and it can take your stop! Up to you buy mark up some charts if you like and we can discuss further. I know that a few of my good friends here like Staurum, Gregg Hoeschec have a sound understanding of this. So hopefully a few of us can comment on what you come up with. That's why on the first time back to a flag you see the upper and the lower Flag Limits as a Reaction Zone. This are only my 2 cents of course, but that's the conclusion I came to by watching how price reacts to zones and where price reacts to! Please Staurum or Master Harry, correct me if I'm wrong. I don't quit Posts: 488 Thank you received: 762 Below is H1 chart, and I started this exercise when price was still around Point 1 Below is the 1-min chart around Point 1: Next we look into FL2, which is created after engulfing FL1: HOME EDUCATION FORUM MORE LOGOUT Going forward, we see FL3 created after engulfing FL2, and then FL4 created after engulfing FL3. Notice that there is another FL that is stacked immediately above FL3, I didn't draw rectangle for it because I wanted to highlight FL3, which according to my hypothesis, is more significant. On the above chart, I have also highlighted in green 3 locations (1, 2, and 3) that price returned to the MPL of each FL and then turned around. Had we taken these 3 trades, with the SL below the outer limit of each FL, we would have doubled our account in 1 day. But of course... hindsight is always perfect. Still struggling to reconcile the rules w.r.t the validation of an FL, that (1)An FL is only valid AFTER price has hit an opposing FL. (2)If price touches an opposing FL upon the creation of a new FL, then this new FL is not valid until price reach the next opposing FL. If I follow these rules to the pip, I would often see that I am not able to draw a new FL that engulfs an old FL. Perhaps this is something that IF thought it's kindergarten and everyone should be able to see it clearly. Essentially, a Flag Limit is a smaller time scale FLAG. The limit of a FLAG is not always delineated by a kink, it can be delineated by a CAP (a RBD/DBR). H[/quote] Posts: 197 Hi Hoto, Thank you received: For me a broken FL is just Broke... If I understand the FTR concept 333 correctly, after price engulfs something important like a FL, it tries to return to origin of the drop/rally and fails. I may not have the best definition of FTR, but for me, if that area that failed does not print a new low/high then it is no FTR and I will steer away from it. Also an FTR can relate to any other important area, be it SR, SD, Swap, another FTR or even a FL. But... IMHO an FTR to a FL has to happen before that FL breaks. FTR should highlight bullish/bearish strength, so it has to happen before the opponent takes control. Now as far as my diagram above is concerned, I was just trying to highlight the relationship of price (after a break of FL) to the limits of that same FL once price retraces back into it in the future. It was just an observation I wanted to share with everyone. It was not meant to confuse anyone... Here is the chart I was tearing apart at the time... So, this came into my head. Offline I shall speak my brains.... Associate Trader What...Me? 1. Here's the pole, big buying Posts: 463 2. Price flags on the way up - we should look for a long entry on the FTB to Thank you received: this 3. Price makes a more local flag, here - likewise, could be a long on the 910 return. Price creates a high from here. 4. Here we have the FTB to the local flag - long opportunity 5. The target for the long is back up into the previous high. Now we don't know what's going to happen. Price could break the previous highs, or it may drop to break the lows created by 3. We don't know, we have to wait (on this time frame, anyway). 6. Price returns to the flag, but we don't get a signal to do anything - we trade from the edges of flags/ranges, not the middle. 7. Oh, come on! I'm getting bored, now... OK, so now we know it was a fakeout, as the IT selling has now engulfed the flag at 3, and is now also the FTB to the flag at 2. Wow. So, we take a long here, targeting the high at 7. 9. The ITs are protecting their position at 7 (where they made the fakeout) and sell right through the flags at 2 and 3, and the low at 8. That's a strong engulf, and now 9 becomes a pretty good FTR. 10. Price flags just under the engulfed area, as it decides what to do next 11. Price breaks down, but does not reach the base of the pole (Aaron ) and so we should look for a short on the FTB to the flag at 10. 12. here's the FTB to that flag. 13. Our target for the short is the low made at 11 14. Errr, it's usually 13 that's missing from airliner rows, etc. Oops. 15. Price has cut right through the supply at 10, and has become demand - we should look to take a long at the top of the zone created by 10. 16. The target for that long is the superb FTR created at 9. We also look to take a short at 16, aiming for the base of the pole. 17. We need to be careful (maybe take some profit) as price returns down to the demand at the 15 flag. In this case it cuts right through. It might even give chance for another short from the underside of the flag 18. The engulf of 2 and 10 by the move to 11 gives us the confidence to aim for 18 as the ultimate target. Posts: 168 Thank you received: What happens when a FL is engulfed? Engulfed FL is a good sign Price wants to fill the base of the FL pole. This 384 is something I like to use as criteria for an FTR trade setup. Why do some FTB trades at FL's work and others don't? A FLAG should break a key level/area to be considered significant. When a bases pole has momentum coming out of a significant price level, SD Zone, SR Flip, etc, and the FL engulfs a key level/area (SR, SD, FL), this is criteria that is important when considering entering on RT to the FL area. Posts: 941 EDUCATION FORUM MORE LOGOUT after the fact its easier to spot them as you understand, so in real time Thank you reHcOeiMveEd: some are cleaner than others. just work with what you have each time. 2920 ok, for flag limits two things are important. as IF said "they signify the end of the momentum" and also we look for them at previous important areas, like obvious SR for example. why? because after the pole, price tries to get back into the area and fails, making a decision and this is our flag limit. so on first return of the price, since the decision has already been made, we can expect a reaction. also, the flag limit area may hold for more tries than the first visit and is valid till broken (but i dont advise anyone to trade it a 2nd time) after the flag limit is engulfed price is free to travel back to the base of the pole, like in Hotochin's example. Some say this is manipulation, but I think that manipulation is part of the Price Action and Order Flow, in the end they are the ones that move the market, not us. I don't have all the solutions but hopefully what I've Associate Trader learned is of some help. First, about the significance of flag limits...some of them are more "localized" flag limits. For example, FL1 is an engulf of a Posts: 196 local high, while FL2 is more of an engulf of the flag area to the left (where Thank you received: we see price meandering around without any new poles). To me that tells me FL2 is probably the more significant than FL1 since we're engulfing a 350 larger zone. FL3 is another story of price engulfing a smaller flag area, but it did work nicely several times as you see. Now onto the more difficult question which I've been searching for as well...FL2 - was it engulfed or not? I don't think so. First, I'm not entirely sure that FL2 is the actual flag limit or not. On the M1 chart where you can't zoom much farther unless you have a tick chart, it's possible that the actual FL extends closer to the "SR" area. If it doesn't and price did move below it, I still see this as an FTR which would show up on higher time frames as a FL in its own right (they are the same thing). Note how price broke above the S/R, tried to get back in, and then moved above the original breakout high, confirming an FTR. Where would I place the stop? Well, I wouldn't have been completely comfortable with that original FL2 zone for previously mentioned reasons, but if I were, I would have placed it a pip or so below the base of it given this is an M1 chart. If I were stopped out, I would have probably given the FTR a try as well since it's valid too. Others might put it beyond the S/R but that isn't something I care to do. Note how in your bottom center graphic that FL2 may have been exceeded by a pip or so but if you use the FTR area it would have stayed within bounds. Significance of FL/FTR has nothing to do with time but with what kind of flag area was engulfed. Are we looking at a strong engulf of a huge daily flag area or are we looking at price engulfing a local flag on the M1? That's what makes the difference in my experience. Keep in mind this is just my two cents, but I hope it helps. This is an area of interest for me as well. The following user(s) said Thank You: rcmacf, akifusenet Feeling the Bern. Thank you received: EDUCATION FORUM MORE LOGOUT 135 HOME Hi John, this question is bothering many of us, including me. The problem is, we are looking for perfection, for something what works 100% of the time. I think, one is only wasting the time doing it. How many weeks, months, years are we wasting looking for answers in forums with clear rules wich work 100% of the time? This is a process oriented approach and you have some very good rules here which you have to build on. But to do, you have to do your own research. There is no way around it. No short cuts. If you take one rule from marketpedia and and go over charts and use the rule in a consistent manner (you use this rule the same way every time), you will get results in terms of if it works or not, in which circumstances etc. You then come to the conclusion, how to trade it. If it for example doesn't work 80% of the time, that's perfect, because you know that when you do the opposite, it will work What I am trying to say is, stop wasting the time searching for perfection and start working on your own unique style, which will work for you and which you will understand because you have built it from the scratch. The process counts. The other thing which is stopping us from improving is the endless searching for 100% accuracy, when there simply is no need for 100% accuracy. We have to accept that we won't be right every time and that is fine because we can still make money. Take something what you think you understand or what you like and do as detailed research on it as you can, then build on it. The following user(s) said Thank You: cuimingzhao THANK YOU QUICK REPLY REPLY QUOTE HOME EDUCATION FORUM MORE LOGOUT Flag Limits 02 Mar 2015 21:00 #807 smimon Whilst it is true that a FL is formed after the break of any high or low, it does not necessarily make it an important FL. The important ones are the ones that form after the break of important opposing levels. Offline In your chart - what is the significance of the green box? What important opposing level was broken that led to its formation? I see you've drawn on Trader a small box that it broke - presumably off something on M1 - but do you think that the break of a small M1 level is as important as the break of the Posts: 549 highs to the left, at which price spent a long time? Not trying to be Thank you received: patronising, forgive me if it comes off that way, but just trying to get you to think about it. "Look left, and then look left again" is a great IF quote. 1075 Here's the AU move as I see it: Remember, spotting important levels is only half of the battle. Reading the movement of price as well is what gives us the context on which to base decisions. Just a zone by itself is only half of the equation. Try not to get too hung up on "needing" to always find exact single tiny FLs on M1. You will drive yourself mad. Instead, find the big obvious ones on higher timeframes, draw a box around the whole FL, and try to focus on just reading the movement of price as it approaches, and look for any surges that give us a clue to when the big boys have entered the market. How did it approach the zone? Did it surge into it? Did it CP? What was the direction of the last large surge in price, bullish or bearish? Have we reached the best level to turn price from, and therefore can we expect a FO? Have we reached the base of the move yet? Is the FL we are looking HOME EDUCATION FORUM MORE LOGOUT at inside daily supply/demand? H4? Weekly? Remember the RTM method is pieces of a jigsaw which all must be pieced together to make full sense of price movement. Focusing exclusively on just one part will cause you to miss the bigger picture. Quite often if we are patient, price will tell us what it wants to do, and we can just get along for the ride. Posts: 106 It can be confusing at first, hopefully this will clear it up for you. Plus it won't Thank you received: hurt to re-read the FTR article 171 FLs are not exactly FTRs. FL's contain FTRs. FL's ecompass the whole HOME EDUCATION FORUM MORE LOGOUT range of hesitation after engulf. FTR's are decision points within FL to continue. FTR's are decision points that happen either before or after engulf. So, for FLs we are interested in DP to continue after engulf. Naturally, when there is an engulf, we can find an FTR (a DP to engulf), and then we can find a FL, that contains a DP to continue (which is also an FTR, but we say it's an FL to point out the difference). Sometimes we can't find an FL, because we have a fakeout and price reverses. HOME EDUCATION FORUM MORE LOGOUT Yes so price retested that CP because the break of a CP makes also an FTR, and price bounced from there down. To trade a FL you have to do what the price reading article says, you have to dissect the level in LTF to make sure there are still some orders left there and also the HTF picture. Then of course watch the approach to the level in LTF for clues like compression, engulfs etc... As you see to do this, you need all the other pieces of this puzzle (CP, engulf, QM,...). Just focus on each one until you can identify them without troubles and then once you know your tools you can study how they interact with each other. Brox wrote: Jurij, you have marked a blue rectangle. But isn't it a FTR? And red line on the second screenshort. Price breaks it and Fails to Return. I am marking only FLs Yes sure it is also an FTR. Every FL is also an FTR, but not every FTR is a FL, this is what has been said many times around in the forums here. FTR means only that price broke some kind of barrier (SR, FL, just a high/low, supply/demand, swap zone) and failed to return (meaning, failed to return back inside that broken zone). My thoughts coincide with 2) - "we don't actually know which set of orders in the flag limit may turn price. It could either be the mouth, body or MPL". Of course as is mentioned the MPL is absolutely the best trade, and I mostly prefer to wait for these orders as well, but we have no guarantees that price will reach the last remaining orders there. If I am to take a trade at the mouth of a FL, it will depend on the size of the FL; with good space provided by PA to allow a trade down to a first target, and a tight FL, we have the luxury of a smaller stop loss, - since whatever the scenario, one thing is certain, my stop must go above the FL we're reacting to. For larger FLs, I'd much rather wait for the MPL of the FL. This is mainly for trade management, and keeping my stops tighter. With nothing to the left, I don't yet see a reason why we can assume that price will necessarily want the MPL, when the ITs may well have all their orders filled by the time price hits the kink to the mouth of the FL, or any possible free pockets of liquidity in the body on the way to the MPL.. This is where I am at with my thinking on this, and of course welcome more thoughts and opinions to build a solid framework for all of this!
